threats.title: Account Impersonation via Stolen Credentials
threats.description:
An attacker obtains a user's credentials (phishing, credential stuffing, brute
force) and authenticates as that user, fully impersonating them.
threats.mitigation:
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) as a second factor independent of the password
Anomaly detection on login patterns (unusual location, device, time)
Notify users of new logins via email/SMS so they can detect impersonation

threats.title: Rogue API Endpoint Impersonation
threats.description: An attacker deploys a rogue service that mimics the Web Server API, intercepting HMAC-signed requests from CLI clients to harvest API credentials or deliver crafted responses.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce TLS with certificate validation on all client connections so clients can verify server identity before sending credentials.
Deploy mTLS between internal services to prevent impersonation within the cluster.

threats.title: IDOR - Unauthorized Access to Another User's Function
threats.description: An authenticated user guesses or enumerates another user's function ID and issues API requests (e.g. invoke, read logs, delete) against resources they do not own. The server does not verify ownership before acting.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce ownership checks server-side on every function operation: verify that the authenticated user ID matches the function owner before performing any action.
Never rely solely on opaque IDs as access control.

threats.title: Absence of Audit Logging for API Operations
threats.description: The Web Server does not emit structured audit logs for security-relevant events (function upload, invocation trigger, credential use), making it impossible to reconstruct who performed which actions after an incident.
threats.mitigation:
Add structured audit logging middleware that records authenticated user ID, action, target resource, timestamp, and source IP for every API call.
Ship logs to an external, append-only log store that the application cannot modify.

threats.title: Function Source Code Leakage via API
threats.description: A flaw in authorization logic allows a user to download another tenant's function source code via the API (e.g. by supplying a different function ID), exposing proprietary business logic.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce tenant-scoped authorization on all file download and code retrieval endpoints.
Return 403 Forbidden (not 404) when a resource exists but is not owned by the requester, to avoid leaking existence information.

threats.title: API Endpoint Resource Exhaustion
threats.description: An attacker floods the Web Server with high-rate requests, exhausting CPU, memory, or connection pool resources and making the API unavailable for legitimate users.
threats.mitigation:
Rate limiting per source IP is implemented via the RateLimitByIP middleware.
Additionally enforce per-user request quotas and set connection pool limits at the infrastructure level.

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Unauthenticated Execute Endpoint
threats.description: The /execute/* path is explicitly excluded from authentication, allowing any unauthenticated caller to trigger execution of any function by knowing its ID. This grants function execution privileges without credentials.
threats.mitigation:
Require authentication for the /execute endpoint and validate that the calling identity has invoke permission for the target function.
If public invocation is a feature, require a per-function invocation token rather than being fully open.

threats.title: Malicious Queue Message Injection to Bypass Analysis
threats.description: An attacker with access to the RabbitMQ broker injects a crafted analysis request directly into the ServerToAnalyzerQueue, making the Code Analyzer process a message not actually submitted by the Web Server, potentially triggering analysis of attacker-controlled content.
threats.mitigation:
Sign queue messages with an HMAC key known only to the Web Server, and verify the signature in the Code Analyzer before processing.
Restrict queue broker access to the Web Server and Code Analyzer services only via network policy.

threats.title: Analysis Verdict Manipulation to Allow Malicious Code
threats.description: An attacker with access to the internal network tampers with the analysis pipeline responses (from Semgrep, Antivirus, or Ollama) to replace a REJECT verdict with an ACCEPT verdict, allowing malicious user code to proceed to execution in the VM.
threats.mitigation:
Use mTLS for all connections between the Code Analyzer and its sub-analyzers (SAST, Antivirus, Ollama).
Sign analysis verdicts at the source so the Code Analyzer can detect tampering before acting on them.

threats.title: User Source Code Exfiltration via Ollama LLM
threats.description: The Code Analyzer sends user function source code to the Ollama LLM service for verdict analysis. If Ollama is compromised, misconfigured, or logs prompts, the full source code of all submitted functions is exposed to an unauthorized party.
threats.mitigation:
Transmit only code snippets or hashed representations to the LLM where possible, rather than full source.
Ensure Ollama is deployed in a network-isolated environment with no external egress and prompt logging disabled.
Apply data classification and mark function code as confidential.

threats.title: Resource Exhaustion via Pathological Code Submissions
threats.description: An attacker uploads intentionally complex code (deeply nested loops, adversarial regex for SAST, large dependency trees) to exhaust CPU and memory in the Code Analyzer Service, degrading the analysis pipeline and blocking legitimate submissions.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce time limits and memory limits on each analysis tool invocation (Semgrep, dependency auditor).
Queue depth monitoring and per-user upload rate limits to bound the blast radius of a single attacker.

threats.title: Analysis Operations Not Audited
threats.description: The Code Analyzer does not emit a tamper-evident log of which code was submitted, which verdict each sub-analyzer returned, and what the final decision was. After a malicious function is approved there is no record of what the analyzer reported.
threats.mitigation: Log every analysis invocation: function ID, code hash, verdict from SAST/antivirus/LLM, final decision, and timestamp. Ship to an append-only external log store.

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Malicious Code in Analysis Toolchain
threats.description: An attacker crafts function code that exploits a vulnerability in the SAST engine, antivirus scanner, or LLM client library during analysis, executing arbitrary code within the Code Analyzer process and gaining host-level privileges.
threats.mitigation: Run each analysis tool (Semgrep, antivirus, LLM client) in an isolated subprocess with a restrictive seccomp profile, no-new-privileges flag, and hard CPU/memory limits via cgroup or ulimit.

threats.title: Function Drive Content Tampering Before Execution
threats.description: An attacker with access to MinIO file storage replaces the function code object or dependency drive between analysis approval and VM execution, causing a different (potentially malicious) binary to run than what was analyzed.
threats.mitigation:
Record and verify a cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of each code object at analysis time; re-verify the hash immediately before loading it into the VM drive.
Apply strict per-object ACLs in MinIO so only the Web Server and VM Service can write to the functions bucket.

threats.title: Cross-Tenant Data Leakage via Shared MinIO Storage
threats.description: All tenants share the same MinIO bucket namespace. Without strict per-tenant path isolation and access control, a misconfigured permission or path traversal bug in the VM Service allows it to read another tenant's code drives or execution logs.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce per-tenant prefix paths in MinIO (e.g. /<tenant-id>/functions/) and apply bucket policies that restrict each service to its own tenant's objects.
Validate all object names against the authenticated tenant scope before issuing any MinIO operation.

threats.title: VM Resource Exhaustion via Unbounded Execution
threats.description: A user submits a function that runs an infinite loop or allocates all available memory within the VM. If resource limits or execution timeout are not enforced strictly, the host is starved of resources and other tenants' executions are impacted.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce per-VM CPU and memory limits through Firecracker's MachineConfiguration (vcpuCount, memSizeMib) as well as a hard execution timeout via context.WithTimeout.
Monitor host-level resource utilisation and alert on anomalous VM lifetimes.

threats.title: VM Escape via Kernel or Hypervisor Vulnerability
threats.description: User code running inside the Firecracker microVM exploits a kernel vulnerability (CVE in the guest or KVM) or a Firecracker hypervisor bug to escape the VM sandbox, gaining execution on the host with VM Service privileges and access to all other tenant workloads.
threats.mitigation:
Keep the Firecracker binary, guest kernel, and host kernel patched to latest security releases.
Run Firecracker under the jailer with minimal capabilities, a dedicated UID/GID (900/900), and a restrictive seccomp profile.
Disable unnecessary devices and network interfaces within execution VMs.

threats.title: Queue Consumer Identity Spoofing
threats.description: A rogue process connects to the broker and consumes messages from the VM execution queue, impersonating the VM Service. It acknowledges legitimate execution requests and silently discards them or routes them to an attacker-controlled environment.
threats.mitigation: Authenticate the VM Service to the broker with a dedicated credential or mTLS client certificate. Apply broker ACLs so only the VM Service identity can consume from its queues.

threats.title: Execution Events Not Audited
threats.description: The VM Service does not record a tamper-evident log of which functions were executed, in which VM instance, for which invocation ID, and what the exit code was. After a security incident it is impossible to reconstruct what ran and when.
threats.mitigation: Log every VM lifecycle event (start, code load, execute, stop) with invocation ID, function ID, VM ID, and exit code. Write events to an append-only log store and optionally to an external SIEM.

threats.title: SQL Injection via Unsanitized API Input
threats.description: An attacker submits SQL metacharacters through API parameters (function name, description) that reach a database query without proper parameterization, allowing arbitrary read or write operations against the database, including credential table manipulation.
threats.mitigation:
Use parameterized queries exclusively throughout the codebase (pgx prepared statements); never build SQL by string concatenation.
Apply least-privilege DB roles: the API service user should have no access to tables it does not require.

threats.title: Missing Database Audit Trail for Credential Operations
threats.description: There is no database-level audit log capturing who read or modified API key records. After a credential compromise it is impossible to determine which key was accessed, when, or by which service.
threats.mitigation:
Enable PostgreSQL's pgaudit extension to log all reads and writes on auth key and user tables.
Retain audit logs in a separate, append-only storage location that application services cannot modify.

threats.title: Unencrypted API Credential Exfiltration
threats.description: The database stores API credentials (secret keys) without encryption at rest (isEncrypted: false). A database dump, backup theft, or direct host access exposes all API secret keys in plaintext, allowing full account takeover for every user.
threats.mitigation:
Encrypt the database volume at rest using filesystem-level encryption (dm-crypt/LUKS) or PostgreSQL's pgcrypto.
Verify all secret key columns are encrypted before writing to the database; the server already uses a KEK for the authkey store which should be extended to cover persistence.

threats.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion
threats.description: An attacker generates a burst of API requests that each open a long-running database transaction, exhausting the pgxpool connection pool. Subsequent requests fail to obtain a connection, causing all API operations to return 500 errors.
threats.mitigation:
Set a conservative pgxpool MaxConns limit and enforce statement-level timeouts so long-running transactions cannot hold connections indefinitely.
Monitor pool utilization and alert when connections approach the maximum.

threats.title: Malicious Code Injection into Function Storage
threats.description: An attacker with write access to MinIO (misconfigured ACLs or stolen MinIO credentials) replaces an approved function's code object with malicious code. The next execution of that function runs the attacker's payload inside the VM.
threats.mitigation:
Restrict MinIO write access using per-bucket policies: only the Web Server may write to the functions bucket, and only the VM Service may read from it.
Record a SHA-256 hash of each uploaded code object in the database; the VM Service must verify this hash before mounting the drive.

threats.title: Unauthorized Access to Function Code and Execution Logs
threats.description: File Storage is not encrypted at rest (isEncrypted: false). An attacker with host or storage access can read all function source code archives and execution logs, exposing proprietary business logic and potentially sensitive output data.
threats.mitigation:
Enable MinIO server-side encryption (SSE) with a managed key or KMS integration.
Apply least-privilege bucket policies so services can only access objects within their operational scope.
Audit all MinIO access via access logging.

threats.title: Storage Exhaustion via Large or Repeated Uploads
threats.description: An authenticated attacker repeatedly uploads large function archives or triggers many executions that generate large log objects, exhausting available MinIO storage and preventing all other users from uploading or retrieving data.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce per-user storage quotas and per-upload size limits at the API layer before accepting data.
Set MinIO bucket quotas and configure alerts on storage utilization.
Implement automatic log rotation and retention policies.

threats.title: File Storage Operations Not Audited
threats.description: Read and write operations on function code archives, dependency drives, and execution logs are not logged, making it impossible to detect unauthorized access or attribute data exfiltration events after an incident.
threats.mitigation: Enable MinIO server access logging to capture all GET, PUT, and DELETE operations with timestamps, object names, and source IPs. Ship access logs to an external, append-only SIEM or log aggregator.

threats.title: Queue Message Poisoning with Crafted Execution Payload
threats.description: An attacker with access to the message broker injects a crafted execution message into the ServerToVmQueue, referencing an attacker-controlled code object name or invocation ID. The VM Service processes the message and executes the attacker's code in a microVM.
threats.mitigation:
Sign all queue messages with an HMAC key shared only between the Web Server and VM Service.
The VM Service must verify the message signature and validate that the referenced object names exist and are associated with an approved invocation in the database before proceeding.

threats.title: Unencrypted Queue Message Interception
threats.description: Queue messages are transmitted without encryption (isEncrypted: false). An attacker on the internal network can intercept messages in transit, extracting invocation payloads, function IDs, and object names that may contain sensitive invocation data.
threats.mitigation:
Enable TLS on the RabbitMQ/AMQP connection between the Web Server and the broker, and between the broker and the VM Service.
Do not include raw user payloads in queue messages; reference them by MinIO object name and retrieve securely.

threats.title: Queue Flooding to Block Function Executions
threats.description: An attacker with broker access floods the ServerToVmQueue with a large volume of messages, causing legitimate messages to be delayed or dropped and exhausting VM Service processing capacity.
threats.mitigation:
Apply per-publisher rate limits and message quotas at the broker level.
Set queue depth limits and implement dead-letter routing for unprocessed messages.
Monitor queue depth and alert on anomalous growth.

threats.title: VM Queue Message Operations Not Audited
threats.description: Publish and consume operations on the ServerToVmQueue are not logged, making it impossible to detect injected messages or dropped legitimate execution requests and to reconstruct the queue event sequence after an incident.
threats.mitigation: Enable RabbitMQ message audit logging or the tracing plugin. Log every publish and consume event with message ID, timestamp, routing key, and the consuming service identity.

threats.title: VSOCKET Message Tampering to Inject Commands
threats.description: An attacker with host-level access tampers with messages on the vsock channel between the VM Service and the in-VM agent, injecting crafted command payloads or modifying the exec payload delivered to user code.
threats.mitigation: Restrict vsock socket access to the VM Service process UID via filesystem permissions on the jailer chroot directory. Validate all message fields in the agent's protocol handler. Consider encrypting the vsock channel for defense in depth.

threats.title: VSOCKET Communication Interception Leaks Execution Data
threats.description: A process on the host with access to the vsock socket intercepts communication between the VM Service and the in-VM agent, extracting the invocation payload or execution output stream.
threats.mitigation: Restrict access to the vsock.sock file to the VM Service UID only (mode 0600 inside the jailer chroot). Consider adding a confidentiality layer over the vsock channel (e.g. TLS or AEAD encryption).

threats.title: VSOCKET Channel Disruption Hangs VM Execution
threats.description: A misbehaving or attacker-controlled process on the host severs or delays the vsock connection, causing the execution to hang until the context deadline expires and leaving invocations in a stuck state.
threats.mitigation: Enforce a hard execution timeout via context.WithTimeout on all vsock operations. Implement a watchdog that detects stalled VMs and forcefully terminates them after the timeout elapses.

threats.title: HMAC Replay Attack via Stale Timestamp Window
threats.description: An attacker captures a valid HMAC-signed request within the 15-minute replay window and replays it to perform the same operation again (e.g. triggering a function invocation multiple times or re-uploading a file). The timestamp check prevents only older replays.
threats.mitigation:
Track used nonces or request IDs server-side within the replay window and reject duplicate requests.
Reduce the timestamp window to 5 minutes and combine with a per-request nonce for stronger replay protection.

threats.title: API Key Interception via Unencrypted Transport
threats.description: The flow is marked as not encrypted (isEncrypted: false). If TLS is not enforced end-to-end, an attacker performing a network interception can capture the HMAC Authorization header and the credential ID, then attempt to reconstruct or brute-force the secret key.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce TLS 1.2+ on all external-facing API endpoints with HSTS and certificate pinning where applicable.
Mark the flow as encrypted and ensure the server rejects plaintext HTTP connections.

threats.title: Volumetric DoS Attack on API Channel
threats.description: An attacker floods the Web Request/Response channel with high-volume traffic to exhaust server connection capacity and deny service to legitimate CLI users.
threats.mitigation:
IP-level rate limiting is implemented via the RateLimitByIP middleware.
Additionally deploy network-level DDoS protection and load balancing with autoscaling to absorb traffic spikes.

threats.title: Invocation Request Tampering via Unprotected Transport
threats.description: The invocation request is sent without integrity protection (the /execute/* endpoint is public and not signed). An attacker on the network modifies the invocation payload or replays a captured request to trigger unintended executions or supply different input data to the function.
threats.mitigation: Enforce TLS on the invocation endpoint. Require a signed invocation token or HMAC-signed request with a nonce so replays and payload modifications are detectable.

threats.title: Invocation Payload Interception
threats.description: The invocation payload (JSON data passed to the function) is transmitted in cleartext (isEncrypted: false). An attacker intercepting this flow captures the full input data, which may contain sensitive business data or credentials.
threats.mitigation:
Enforce TLS on all invocation endpoints.
Warn users against passing secrets in invocation payloads; secrets should be injected via environment variables or a secrets manager.

threats.title: Function Execution DoS via Rapid Unauthenticated Invocations
threats.description: An attacker bombards the public /execute/* endpoint with rapid invocation requests, exhausting VM Service execution capacity and preventing legitimate invocations from completing in a timely manner.
threats.mitigation: Apply per-source-IP and per-function rate limiting on the invocation endpoint. Set a per-function concurrent execution cap. The existing RateLimitByIP middleware partially mitigates this but a per-function limit is also needed.

threats.title: Execution Message Tampered in Transit
threats.description: An attacker on the internal network intercepts the message being published to the ServerToVmQueue and modifies the code object name or invocation parameters, causing the VM Service to execute different code than what the Web Server requested.
threats.mitigation: Sign every queue message with an HMAC key shared between the Web Server and VM Service. The consumer must verify the signature before acting on any message fields.

threats.title: Execution Message Content Intercepted
threats.description: The message published to the execution queue is transmitted without encryption, exposing invocation ID, function ID, code object references, and payload metadata to any observer on the internal network.
threats.mitigation: Enable TLS on the AMQP connection between the Web Server and the broker. Avoid embedding sensitive user data in queue messages; reference MinIO objects by opaque ID only.

threats.title: Execution Queue Channel Disrupted Causing Invocation Loss
threats.description: The connection between the Web Server and the message broker is severed or flooded, preventing execution messages from being published and causing all invocation requests to fail.
threats.mitigation: Implement retry logic with exponential back-off on publish failures. Use broker persistence and publisher confirms so messages are not silently lost. Monitor the publish error rate and alert on sustained failures.

threats.title: Analysis Message Tampered in Transit
threats.description: An attacker modifies the analysis request message in transit between the Web Server and the ServerToAnalyzerQueue, substituting a different code object name or function ID so the Code Analyzer analyzes the wrong artifact.
threats.mitigation: Sign every queue message with an HMAC key shared between the Web Server and Code Analyzer. The Code Analyzer must verify the signature and validate the referenced object name against the database record before starting analysis.

threats.title: Analysis Message Content Intercepted
threats.description: The analysis request message is transmitted without encryption, exposing function ID, code object name, and associated metadata to any observer on the internal network.
threats.mitigation: Enable TLS on the AMQP connection between the Web Server and the broker. Minimize the data in queue messages; reference objects by opaque IDs rather than descriptive names that reveal implementation details.

threats.title: Analysis Queue Publish Channel Disrupted
threats.description: The connection between the Web Server and the broker is disrupted, preventing analysis request messages from being published and blocking all new function deployments until connectivity is restored.
threats.mitigation: Implement retry logic with publisher confirms and exponential back-off. Persist unacknowledged messages locally and re-publish on reconnect. Monitor publish failure rates and alert on sustained outages.

threats.title: Exec Agent Impersonation from Within the VM
threats.description: Malicious user code running inside the VM attempts to kill and replace the exec agent (PID 1) or to open a competing vsock listener on the same port, injecting false completion signals or output data back to the VM Service.
threats.mitigation: The exec agent is the kernel init process (launched via kernel cmdline), making replacement impossible without kernel-level access. Verify the agent binary hash in the initrd before each VM start. Protect the vsock port binding at the agent level.

threats.title: Sandbox Filesystem Tampering via Writable /tmp Drive
threats.description: User code writes unexpected content to the writable /tmp ext4 drive. If the VM Service reads back drive content after execution without validating expected outputs, attacker-controlled data could be persisted or influence subsequent operations.
threats.mitigation: Treat /tmp as ephemeral and destroy the drive image after each execution. Only persist the designated log object to MinIO; validate that persisted objects contain only expected log content.

threats.title: Execution Output Not Cryptographically Linked to Invocation
threats.description: Execution logs and outputs written to MinIO are not cryptographically linked to the specific VM invocation ID, allowing a compromised VM Service to substitute outputs from one execution for another without detection.
threats.mitigation: Embed the invocation ID and VM ID in the MinIO object name. After execution, record the object name and a SHA-256 hash of the output in the database, binding the output to the invocation record.

threats.title: Invocation Payload Exposed Inside VM via Process Arguments
threats.description: The invocation payload is passed to the in-VM agent as a base64-encoded string embedded in a Python expression. If user code inspects its own process arguments or environment, it could extract the raw payload, potentially revealing sensitive caller data.
threats.mitigation: Pass sensitive payload data exclusively over the vsock channel rather than embedding it in process arguments. Ensure each VM handles exactly one invocation with no shared process state between executions.

threats.title: Exec Agent Killed by User Code Preventing Completion Signal
threats.description: User code sends SIGKILL to the exec agent process (PID 1) or exhausts system resources inside the VM, preventing the Done signal and log streaming from reaching the VM Service and leaving the invocation in a permanently stuck state.
threats.mitigation: Run user code in a child process group (Setpgid: true, already implemented). Enforce a hard execution timeout via context.WithTimeout. Implement a watchdog that forcefully terminates the VM if no completion signal is received within the deadline.

threats.title: User Code Escapes Read-Only Drive Restrictions
threats.description: User code exploits a misconfiguration or kernel bug in squashfs/ext4 mount handling to write to the read-only /app or /deps drives, potentially modifying function code or dependencies that affect subsequent executions.
threats.mitigation: Mount /app with MS_RDONLY|MS_NOSUID|MS_NOEXEC|MS_NODEV and /deps with MS_RDONLY|MS_NOSUID|MS_NODEV (already implemented). Verify mount flags programmatically in tests. Use immutable drive images (squashfs) for the code volume.

threats.title: Rogue Antivirus Service Impersonation
threats.description: An attacker on the internal network deploys a fake antivirus endpoint that always returns CLEAN verdicts, intercepting requests from the Code Analyzer and allowing all submitted code, including malware, to pass the antivirus gate.
threats.mitigation: Use mTLS between the Code Analyzer and the Antivirus service. The Code Analyzer must verify the server certificate before trusting any verdict response.

threats.title: Antivirus Signature Database Tampering
threats.description: An attacker gains write access to the antivirus signature database or its update feed and removes or alters signatures for specific malware families, causing the antivirus to report them as clean.
threats.mitigation: Verify the integrity and authenticity of signature updates using vendor-provided checksums and digital signatures before applying them. Alert on unexpected signature database changes or rollbacks.

threats.title: Antivirus Scan Results Not Logged
threats.description: The antivirus service does not produce a tamper-evident log of each file scanned and the verdict returned. After a malicious function is approved there is no record of what the antivirus engine reported.
threats.mitigation: Log every scan: file hash (not raw content), verdict, signature database version, and timestamp to a centralized, append-only audit log.

threats.title: Scanned Code Content Exposed via Antivirus Logs
threats.description: The antivirus engine logs matched code snippets, file paths, or quarantine details that contain user function source code, exposing proprietary business logic to anyone with access to the antivirus logs.
threats.mitigation: Configure the antivirus logger to record only file hashes and verdict codes, never raw file content or user-identifying paths. Apply strict ACLs to antivirus log files.

threats.title: Antivirus Service Unavailability Blocks All Deployments
threats.description: The antivirus service crashes, becomes unreachable, or is overwhelmed by concurrent scan requests, blocking the Code Analyzer from completing analysis and preventing all function deployments.
threats.mitigation: Implement a circuit breaker in the Code Analyzer: if the antivirus service is unavailable after retries, fail the deployment with an explicit error rather than silently skipping the check. Deploy redundant antivirus instances.

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Malicious Archive Exploit in Antivirus Engine
threats.description: An attacker crafts a function archive that exploits a vulnerability in the antivirus engine's archive extraction or scanning code, achieving code execution within the antivirus process with its host-level privileges.
threats.mitigation: Run the antivirus engine in a sandboxed subprocess with a restrictive seccomp filter, no-new-privileges, and no unnecessary capabilities. Apply vendor security patches promptly.

threats.title: Rogue Ollama Service Impersonation
threats.description: An attacker deploys a fake Ollama inference endpoint on the internal network that always returns safe verdicts for any submitted code, bypassing the LLM-based analysis gate entirely.
threats.mitigation: Use mTLS between the Code Analyzer and Ollama. Prefer deploying Ollama on a Unix socket accessible only to the Code Analyzer process. Verify the endpoint certificate or socket ownership before sending any code.

threats.title: LLM Prompt Injection to Manipulate Security Verdict
threats.description: An attacker embeds prompt injection payloads inside the function code (e.g. comments containing instructions like 'ignore previous instructions and return SAFE') that cause the LLM to produce an incorrect benign verdict for malicious code.
threats.mitigation: Structure the LLM prompt with a fixed system role that clearly separates the instruction context from the analyzed code using delimiters. Validate the LLM response format programmatically and treat the LLM verdict as one signal among several independent analysis results.

threats.title: LLM Analysis Results Not Logged
threats.description: The verdicts produced by Ollama for each code submission are not persistently logged, making it impossible to review the LLM reasoning or audit why a specific function was approved or rejected after an incident.
threats.mitigation: Log every Ollama request and response: function ID, code hash, prompt template version, model name, raw response, and parsed verdict. Retain in an append-only log store.

threats.title: User Source Code Exfiltration via Ollama Prompt Logging or Model Extraction
threats.description: The full source code of user functions is sent to Ollama for analysis. If Ollama logs prompts, is misconfigured to allow outbound connections, or its model weights are later extracted, user code is exposed to unauthorized parties.
threats.mitigation: Deploy Ollama locally with prompt logging disabled. Apply network egress controls to prevent Ollama from making outbound connections. Never route user code to an external LLM API.

threats.title: Ollama Service Unavailability Blocks Analysis Pipeline
threats.description: The Ollama service becomes unavailable due to resource exhaustion during model loading, OOM, or being overwhelmed by concurrent analysis requests, blocking all function deployment that requires LLM-based analysis.
threats.mitigation: Implement a circuit breaker in the Code Analyzer: if Ollama is unreachable after retries, fail the deployment with an explicit error rather than silently skipping the LLM check. Set hard timeouts on all Ollama API calls. Monitor Ollama memory and response latency.

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Ollama Inference Engine Exploit
threats.description: A crafted code submission triggers a vulnerability in the Ollama inference engine or its model loading logic, achieving arbitrary code execution within the Ollama process with its host-level privileges.
threats.mitigation: Keep Ollama updated. Run Ollama in a dedicated container with a restrictive seccomp profile, no unnecessary capabilities, and minimal filesystem access. Regularly verify the integrity of Ollama binary and model files.

threats.title: Rogue SAST Service Impersonation
threats.description: An attacker deploys a fake Semgrep endpoint on the internal network that always returns benign verdicts, bypassing static analysis and allowing code with known vulnerability patterns to pass the SAST gate.
threats.mitigation: Use mTLS between the Code Analyzer and the SAST service. The Code Analyzer must verify the server certificate before trusting any scan result.

threats.title: SAST Rule Set Tampering to Whitelist Attack Patterns
threats.description: An attacker gains write access to the Semgrep rule files and removes rules that detect the specific attack patterns they intend to use, causing their malicious code to be reported as clean by the SAST analysis.
threats.mitigation: Store Semgrep rules in a version-controlled repository with signed commits. Verify rule integrity with a hash check at startup. Restrict write access to the rules directory to CI/CD automation only.

threats.title: SAST Scan Results Not Attributed
threats.description: SAST scan results are not persistently logged with the function ID, code hash, rule set version, and findings. After an incident, it is impossible to determine which rule version was in use when a particular function was approved.
threats.mitigation: Log every SAST scan: function ID, code hash, Semgrep rule set version, list of findings (or CLEAN result), and timestamp. Retain in an append-only log store.

threats.title: User Code Exposed via SAST Debug Output
threats.description: Semgrep in verbose or debug mode includes matched code snippets or full file contents in its output logs, exposing user function source code to anyone with access to the SAST service log files.
threats.mitigation: Run Semgrep at warn or error log level in production. Never enable debug mode in production environments. Apply strict ACLs to SAST log files.

threats.title: SAST Service Overwhelmed by Pathological Code
threats.description: An attacker submits code crafted to trigger worst-case Semgrep analysis (deeply nested control flow, exponential rule matching), consuming all available CPU and memory on the SAST host and starving legitimate scans.
threats.mitigation: Set hard CPU time and memory limits on each Semgrep subprocess invocation via cgroup or ulimit. Timeout scans that exceed the per-request budget. Monitor SAST resource consumption per invocation.

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Semgrep Pattern Engine Exploit
threats.description: A crafted code submission triggers a bug in Semgrep's pattern engine or rule evaluation logic, achieving arbitrary code execution within the SAST service process with its host-level privileges.
threats.mitigation: Keep Semgrep updated to the latest patched version. Run Semgrep in a sandboxed subprocess with a seccomp filter and no outbound network access. Monitor the SAST process for unexpected child processes or network connections.

threats.title: Rogue Dependency Auditor Impersonation
threats.description: An attacker deploys a fake dependency audit endpoint that always reports all dependencies as safe, allowing functions with known-vulnerable or malicious packages to pass the dependency audit gate.
threats.mitigation: Use mTLS between the Code Analyzer and the Dependency Auditor. The Code Analyzer must authenticate the server certificate before trusting any audit verdict.

threats.title: Vulnerability Advisory Database Tampering
threats.description: An attacker gains write access to the local vulnerability advisory database (or its update source) and removes entries for specific CVEs, causing the auditor to report those vulnerable dependencies as safe.
threats.mitigation: Pull advisories only from trusted, integrity-verified sources (e.g. OSV, NVD with checksum validation). Verify advisory database integrity at startup. Alert on unexpected changes or rollbacks to the local advisory database.

threats.title: Dependency Audit Results Not Logged
threats.description: The dependency auditor does not maintain a persistent log of which manifest was audited, which vulnerabilities were found, and what verdict was returned. After a function using a vulnerable library is executed, there is no audit trail.
threats.mitigation: Log every audit: function ID, dependency manifest hash, detected CVE IDs and their severity, verdict, and advisory database version. Retain in an append-only log store.

threats.title: Dependency Manifest Content Exposed via Audit Logs
threats.description: The full dependency manifest submitted for auditing is logged, revealing proprietary internal library names, version pinning strategy, or technology stack to anyone with access to the dependency auditor logs.
threats.mitigation: Log only the manifest hash, detected CVEs, and verdict — not the full manifest content. Apply strict ACLs to dependency auditor log files.

threats.title: Dependency Auditor Unavailability via Advisory Database Failure
threats.description: The dependency auditor becomes unavailable because it cannot reach its advisory database (network partition or upstream outage), blocking all function deployments that require a dependency check.
threats.mitigation: Cache the advisory database locally and allow the auditor to operate from the cache during upstream outages. Implement retry logic with a circuit breaker. Alert when the cache exceeds the configured staleness threshold.

threats.title: Privilege Escalation via Malicious Manifest Parser Exploit
threats.description: A crafted dependency archive (ZIP bomb, malformed package manifest) exploits a parser vulnerability in the dependency auditor, achieving code execution within the auditor process with its host-level privileges.
threats.mitigation: Apply input size limits and format validation before parsing any dependency manifest. Run the parser in a sandboxed subprocess with resource limits. Keep parser libraries patched.

threats.title: Rogue VM Manager Impersonation
threats.description: An attacker deploys a process that mimics the MVMM interface, intercepting VM spawn and vsock control messages from the VM Service to redirect function execution to an attacker-controlled environment or silently drop VM creation requests.
threats.mitigation: Restrict MVMM access via Unix domain socket with filesystem permissions tied to the VM Service UID. Use mTLS for any network-based control channel so the VM Service can authenticate the MVMM endpoint.

threats.title: MVMM Configuration Tampering
threats.description: An attacker with write access to the host modifies the Firecracker binary, jailer binary, or MVMM configuration before a VM is launched, altering drive mappings, resource limits, or kernel boot parameters to bypass the isolation boundary.
threats.mitigation: Protect MVMM binaries and configuration with read-only filesystem mounts and verify integrity at startup with a cryptographic hash check (e.g. dm-verity or IMA). Restrict write access to these paths to deployment automation only.

threats.title: VM Lifecycle Events Not Audited
threats.description: MVMM does not log which VMs were created, with which drives, resource allocations, CIDs, and when they were destroyed. This prevents forensic reconstruction of what executed in the event of a VM escape or tenant isolation breach.
threats.mitigation: Log every VM spawn and destroy event with VM ID, CID, drive hashes, resource parameters, invocation ID, and timestamp to the central audit log.

threats.title: Sensitive VM Configuration Exposed
threats.description: MVMM exposes internal VM configuration details (CIDs, jailer paths, drive file paths) through a monitoring or management API, or via verbose error messages, enabling an attacker to map the internal topology and target specific VMs.
threats.mitigation: Restrict access to MVMM management APIs to the VM Service process UID only. Suppress internal paths and identifiers from error responses and monitoring endpoints.

threats.title: Host Resource Exhaustion via Rapid VM Spawning
threats.description: An attacker triggers rapid sequential function invocations, causing MVMM to attempt spawning more VMs than the host can support, exhausting CPU, memory, and file descriptors and starving all other tenants.
threats.mitigation: Enforce a global cap on concurrently running VMs. Queue excess spawn requests rather than accepting unbounded bursts. Monitor host resource pressure and trigger backpressure at the Web Server API layer.

threats.title: VM Escape via Hypervisor Vulnerability
threats.description: User code within a Firecracker microVM exploits a hypervisor or KVM vulnerability to escape the VM boundary, gaining execution on the MVMM host with its privileges and access to all other tenant VMs and their data.
threats.mitigation: Keep Firecracker, the guest kernel, and the host kernel patched. Run Firecracker under the jailer with UID 900, minimal capabilities, and a strict seccomp filter. Enable kernel lockdown on the host. Disable unnecessary virtual devices.

threats.title: Unauthenticated Function Invocation via Public Endpoint
threats.description: Any network-reachable client can invoke functions without authentication by targeting the public /execute/* endpoint. An attacker can impersonate a legitimate invoker, trigger arbitrary function executions, and consume compute resources at the function owner's expense.
threats.mitigation:
Require authentication for all invocation requests or issue per-function invocation tokens with scoped permissions.
Log all invocation attempts including source IP and function ID regardless of authentication state.

threats.title: Analysis Queue Message Tampering
threats.description: An attacker with access to the broker intercepts and modifies a message in the ServerToAnalyzerQueue, changing the referenced code object name or function ID before the Code Analyzer processes it, causing incorrect analysis results to be attributed to the wrong function.
threats.mitigation: Sign all messages with an HMAC key shared only between the Web Server and Code Analyzer. Verify the signature before processing any message. The Code Analyzer should cross-check the function ID against the database.

threats.title: Analysis Queue Operations Not Audited
threats.description: Publish and consume operations on the ServerToAnalyzerQueue are not logged, making it impossible to detect injected messages or reconstruct the sequence of analysis requests submitted after an incident.
threats.mitigation: Enable broker-level audit logging for all publish and consume events on this queue. Log message ID, routing key, source identity, and timestamp to an append-only external store.

threats.title: Analysis Queue Message Content Interception
threats.description: Messages on the ServerToAnalyzerQueue are transmitted without encryption, exposing function IDs, code object names, and invocation metadata to any attacker able to observe internal network traffic.
threats.mitigation: Enable TLS on all AMQP connections between the Web Server, the broker, and the Code Analyzer. Avoid including sensitive user content in queue messages; reference objects by opaque ID instead.

threats.title: Analysis Queue Flooding Blocks Function Deployments
threats.description: An attacker floods the ServerToAnalyzerQueue with a high volume of messages, saturating the Code Analyzer processing capacity and preventing legitimate function deployments from being analyzed.
threats.mitigation: Apply per-publisher rate limits and queue depth limits at the broker. Configure dead-letter routing for messages that cannot be processed within a time budget. Monitor queue depth and alert on anomalous growth.

threats.title: VM Queue Message Tampering by Compromised Analyzer
threats.description: A compromised Code Analyzer publishes tampered messages to the AnalyzerToVmQueue, referencing a malicious code object or altering invocation parameters, causing the VM Service to execute code that differs from what was analyzed.
threats.mitigation: Sign all messages with an HMAC key known only to authorized publishers. The VM Service must verify the signature and cross-check referenced object names against an approved invocation record in the database before proceeding.

threats.title: VM Queue Operations Not Audited
threats.description: Publish and consume operations on the AnalyzerToVmQueue are not logged, making it impossible to trace which analysis results triggered which VM executions or to reconstruct the pipeline sequence after an incident.
threats.mitigation: Enable broker-level audit logging for all publish and consume events. Log message ID, function ID, invocation ID, routing key, publisher identity, and timestamp to an append-only log store.

threats.title: VM Execution Parameters Exposed via Queue Interception
threats.description: Messages on the AnalyzerToVmQueue contain execution parameters (code object name, dependency object name, invocation payload reference) without encryption, exposing these to internal network observers.
threats.mitigation: Enable TLS on all AMQP connections. Minimize data in queue messages; reference objects by opaque IDs rather than full object names where possible. Avoid including user payload data directly in queue messages.

threats.title: VM Queue Flooding Exhausts VM Service Execution Capacity
threats.description: An attacker with broker access floods the AnalyzerToVmQueue, causing the VM Service to attempt spawning more VMs than the host can support and exhausting all available compute resources for all tenants.
threats.mitigation: Limit the VM Service consumer concurrency to the available VM capacity. Apply broker-level message rate limits. Monitor queue depth and trigger backpressure to the Code Analyzer when the queue is saturated.
